```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(manifoldalign)
set.seed(5821)
```

SSMA aligns observations through domain-specific linear projections. Additional
knowledge may concern features, groups of features, or averages of observations.
`linear_correspondence()` represents these as weighted linear summaries of the
projection coefficients. It works with unequal feature counts and partial links;
no one-to-one correspondence between entire feature spaces is assumed. SSMA
remains experimental: numerical agreement is not evidence of predictive benefit.

## Objective and coordinate contract

For processed observations $X_s$, let $Y_s=X_sW_s$. A correspondence adds

$$\lambda\sum_q d_q\|(H_sW_s)_q-(H_tW_t)_q\|^2$$

to SSMA's existing objective. It changes neither the observation graph nor its
degree-based normalization. A single-domain `linear_penalty()` instead adds
$\lambda\sum_q d_q\|(H_sW_s)_q\|^2$, useful for smoothness or coefficient contrasts.
These are soft, homogeneous quadratic penalties, not hard equalities.

Maps act on **processed input features, before internal compression**. They are
never centered or standardized as observations. For arbitrary preprocessing,
construct maps in its resulting feature coordinates explicitly; the package does
not guess a raw-to-processed conversion. If $X_{processed}=(X-\mu)S$, a functional
$H$ of raw coefficients becomes $HS$ in processed coordinates. Intercepts are not
part of this coefficient contract. Input-domain names and optional map row/column
names are checked; unnamed map columns have positional semantics.

## Matching feature summaries alongside observations

This generic example links summaries of two measurement systems with five and
seven features. The maps could select homologous genes, average sensor groups,
or describe linear calibration measurements.

```{r fit}
x <- list(a = matrix(rnorm(24 * 5), 24, 5),
          b = matrix(rnorm(27 * 7), 27, 7))
h <- list(matrix(rnorm(4 * 5), 4, 5), matrix(rnorm(4 * 7), 4, 7))
link <- linear_correspondence(
  domains = c("a", "b"), maps = h,
  weights = c(1, 0, 2, 3), strength = 2, name = "measurements"
)
rows <- data.frame(domain_i = 1L, index_i = 1:12,
                   domain_j = 2L, index_j = 2:13)
fit <- ssma_align(
  x, correspondences = rows, constraints = list(link),
  preproc = NULL, ncomp = 3,
  control = ssma_align_control(knn = 8, sigma = 2, compression = "none")
)
fit$constraint_diagnostics
```

`weights` describe confidence in each matched summary. Zero confidence excludes
a row. The default `reduction="weighted_mean"` normalizes confidence weights;
`"sum"` preserves their magnitude. `strength` scales the resulting objective.
Neither operation equalizes map units. Normalize measurement units deliberately,
and choose strengths within the permitted training folds. Multiple objects have
additive objectives. If a family spans many domain pairs, allocate its overall
strength across those pairs explicitly; more pairs otherwise add more weight.

Rows with missing measurements should be omitted from the maps and weights,
not filled with zeros. Named map rows must match in order. Feature names, when
supplied on a map, must match the corresponding processed input in order.

## Observation averages and smooth correspondences

Given averaging matrices $A_s$ and $A_t$, use $H_s=A_sX_s$ and $H_t=A_tX_t$.
Rows can encode weighted windows, interpolation, or a declared temporal smoothing
kernel. One-hot selectors recover ordinary sample-correspondence penalties when
weights and reductions match. Helpers outside the alignment method should choose
the windows and handle boundaries, missing samples, timing, and domain semantics.

Existing `correspondences` continue to support direct observation links. Set
`auto_correspondences=FALSE` when the intended sample graph has no cross-domain
links. This disables label/MNN discovery when explicit links are absent, which is
particularly important when differently sized feature spaces have no common
Euclidean coordinate system. Explicit links still apply.

## Composition with PCA and covariance maps

With $Z_s=X_sP_s$, fit SSMA on $Z_s$, supply maps $H_sP_s$, and recover original
feature coefficients as $W_s=P_sB_s$. This is exact in the retained subspace;
truncation discards information and can change the observation-neighbor graph.
Preserve any scaling or whitening in the composed mapping.

For spatial or grouped-feature summaries $G_s$, $G_sP_s$ constrains averages of
projection coefficients. To constrain averages of covariance fingerprints
$F_s=C_sP_sB_s$, instead supply $G_sC_sP_s$. For centered real observations this
can be computed without a full feature-by-feature covariance matrix:

```{r covariance, eval=FALSE}
z <- x %*% p
h <- (g %*% t(x)) %*% z / (nrow(x) - 1)
fingerprint <- crossprod(x, z %*% b) / (nrow(x) - 1)
```

These are covariance fingerprints, not automatically standardized correlations
or a guarantee that all feature-connectivity distances are preserved. Estimate
covariances from actual observations, respecting nuisance processing, weights,
missingness and validation folds. Projection weights and covariance patterns have
different meanings.

`compression="none"` preserves already reduced features without allocating an
identity basis. With the default internal SVD, the package projects maps through
its basis and returns `compression_bases`; each NULL entry denotes identity.
`discarded_energy_fraction` reports the unweighted Frobenius-energy fraction of
each map outside the retained basis. It is a map-support diagnostic, not neural
variance explained. Rank compression can remove useful constraints: inspect this
quantity rather than assuming anatomical or low-variance directions survived.

## Sparse maps, solvers, diagnostics and validation

Base matrices and numeric `Matrix` maps are accepted. Sparse maps remain sparse
until reduced products require dense values. The operator solver applies maps and
their transposes without assembling the global constraint matrix. The dense solver
forms only reduced blocks. With compression disabled, the caller is responsible
for choosing a manageable input dimension. This is not a streaming data loader.

Diagnostics report active row counts, reduction, strength, effective weight sum,
per-component residuals, total residual and weighted objective contribution for
each named constraint. Small residuals alone do not imply useful alignment: large
strengths can suppress directions and contradictory constraints cannot generally
all be satisfied. Inspect out-of-sample performance and appropriate shuffled-link
controls separately.

The tests include independent outer-product and generalized-eigenproblem
oracles, dense/operator agreement, sample-link equivalence, sparse and unequal
feature spaces, null penalties, truncation, confidence splitting, contradictions,
and permutation/rotation invariants. Fitted domains can be transformed using their
own learned projections. This extension does not create a new-domain adaptation
protocol; any use of an unlabeled target during fitting must be declared.

## Preventing domain amplitude collapse

The usual generalized eigenproblem normalizes scores jointly. It does not
require each domain to contribute to every dimension: a direction may be almost
entirely supplied by one domain. Increasing correspondence strengths cannot
exclude that feasible solution.

The optional `ssma_align_control(normalization = "domain_scores")` instead
minimizes the same graph-plus-constraint quadratic subject to

\[
W_i^\top X_i^\top X_i W_i=I_q \quad\text{for every domain }i.
\]

Here `X_i` denotes the processed data in the retained compression coordinates.
The solver whitens each score Gram matrix and optimizes on a product of Stiefel
manifolds with positive-diagonal Householder QR retractions, projected gradients, safeguarded spectral
steps and monotone Armijo descent. Numerical score-null directions (relative
Gram eigenvalue at most `1e-10`) are fixed to zero: optimization is restricted
to the retained score-metric range. At least `ncomp` independent score directions
are required in every domain. No ridge is used to manufacture score variance.

Use preprocessing appropriate to the scientific estimand. The constraint is an
uncentered score Gram identity; it is a covariance constraint only for centered
processed data. Different sample counts are allowed, with equal **total** score
energy per domain rather than equal per-observation variance.

This is an experimental nonconvex alternative to the global eigenproblem, not
post-hoc normalization of its answer. `solver="operator"` is rejected. The
optimizer errors if `domain_tol` is not reached within `domain_maxiter`; increase
the computational budget explicitly rather than treating a stopped iterate as
a converged fit. Inspect `fit$domain_diagnostics` for tangent-gradient norm,
monotone objective history, score-Gram error and retained score ranks.
`generalized_eigenvalues` is `NULL` because this fit is not a generalized
eigendecomposition. The stationary point has no global-optimum guarantee, and a
common orthogonal rotation of all domains remains unidentified.

Equal score energy is imposed by construction. It does not show that
correspondences are correct, that within-domain geometry is preserved in full,
or that transfer to a held-out domain succeeds. Qualify those properties with
independent correspondences, negative controls and application-specific
held-out evaluation. Keep feature-map composition unchanged: covariance-pattern
features still require `C P W`, rather than interpreting projection weights
`P W` as activation patterns.
